Entire-Checkpoint: 1bf60ad9778e


=== nvim,tmux: paste from the real clipboard on local sessions
A tmux server first started over SSH keeps SSH_TTY and SSH_CLIENT in its
global environment forever - update-environment refreshes SSH_CONNECTION
but not those two - so every later pane inherits them and a local session
looks remote.

clipboard.lua branched on $SSH_TTY and so took the OSC 52 path, whose
paste handler returned register 0. That register only ever holds the last
yank, so p after dd pasted the wrong text. Drop the branching entirely and
let Neovim autodetect the provider (pbcopy on macOS, wl-copy under Wayland,
xclip under X11, OSC 52 only when there is no local clipboard), and add the
two leaking vars to update-environment - which also stops powerlevel10k
showing an SSH prompt on a local session.

import sys
e = open('/sys/class/drm/card1-DP-1/edid','rb').read()
print("EDID bytes:", len(e), "blocks:", 1+e[126])
# base block detailed timings at 54,72,90,108
def dtd(b):
    pc = (b[1]<<8|b[0])*10  # kHz
    if pc == 0: return None
    ha = b[2] | ((b[4]>>4)<<8)
    va = b[5] | ((b[7]>>4)<<8)
    hb = b[3] | ((b[4]&0xf)<<8)
    vb = b[6] | ((b[7]&0xf)<<8)
    ht, vt = ha+hb, va+vb
    refresh = pc*1000/(ht*vt) if ht*vt else 0
    return f"{ha}x{va} pixclk={pc/1000:.3f}MHz refresh={refresh:.2f}Hz  (data rate @8bpc = {pc*1000*24/1e9:.2f} Gbps)"
print("\n-- base block detailed timings (first = PREFERRED) --")
for off in (54,72,90,108):
    d = dtd(e[off:off+18])
    if d: print("  ", d)
# CTA-861 extension
for blk in range(1, 1+e[126]):
    b = e[blk*128:(blk+1)*128]
    if not b or b[0] != 0x02: continue
    print(f"\n-- CTA-861 ext block {blk} (rev {b[1]}) --")
    d = b[2]
    idx = 4
    while idx < d:
        tag = b[idx]>>5; ln = b[idx]&0x1f
        payload = b[idx+1:idx+1+ln]
        if tag == 3:  # vendor specific
            oui = payload[2]<<16 | payload[1]<<8 | payload[0]
            print(f"   VSDB OUI={oui:06X} " + {0x000C03:"<-- HDMI 1.4 (HDMI Licensing LLC)",0xC45DD8:"<-- HDMI 2.0 (HDMI Forum)"}.get(oui,""))
            if oui == 0x000C03 and ln >= 7:
                print(f"     Max TMDS clock = {payload[6]*5} MHz")
            if oui == 0xC45DD8 and ln >= 5:
                print(f"     Max TMDS char rate = {payload[4]*5} MHz")
        idx += 1 + ln
    # detailed timings in ext block
    dof = b[2]
    while dof + 18 <= 127:
        r = dtd(b[dof:dof+18])
        if r: print("   ext DTD:", r)
        dof += 18
PY

content.text:
Nothing in your dotfiles is at fault — no mode is set anywhere, and sway takes the connector's preferred mode. The problem is the DisplayPort link itself.

## What I found

Your monitor and GPU both advertise 4K@60 correctly:

- EDID preferred timing: **3840x2160 @ 60.00Hz, 533.25 MHz pixel clock**, interface = DisplayPort, 10 bpc, HDR
- Kernel lists `3840x2160` first in `/sys/class/drm/card1-DP-1/modes`
- `link-status = 0` (Good) — training succeeded, no error flagged

But when I asked sway for it, it reported `success` and silently stayed at 1440p. 4K@30 applied instantly. That gap is the tell:

| Mode | Payload @8bpc | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 2560x1440@60 | 5.80 Gbps | works |
| 3840x2160@30 | 7.13 Gbps | works |
| 3840x2160@60 | **12.80 Gbps** | **rejected** |

The cutoff sits between 7.13 and 12.8 Gbps. DP link payload capacities over 4 lanes: HBR = **8.64 Gbps**, HBR2 = 17.28 Gbps. Your ceiling lands exactly on HBR. If the link were HBR2, 4K@60 would fit with room to spare (even at 10 bpc, 16.0 Gbps).

**Your DP link is running at HBR (DP 1.1 speed) instead of HBR2.** 4K@60 is physically impossible over that, so wlroots walks down the mode list to 1440p — and since 1440p isn't an integer fraction of 4K, it also looks soft.

## Fixes, cheapest first

1. **Monitor OSD → Settings → General → "DisplayPort Version" → set to 1.2 or 1.4.** LG 4K HDR panels ship this at 1.1 on some firmware, which caps the link at HBR and produces exactly this symptom. Free, 30 seconds, try it first.
2. **Replace the DP cable** with a VESA-certified DP 1.2+ (HBR2) one, ideally under 2 m. Bundled and cheap long cables commonly fail HBR2 training and fall back to HBR.
3. Your `HDMI-A-1` port is free (DP-2, DP-3, HDMI-A-1 all disconnected) if you want to test with a different cable path.

Once the link negotiates HBR2, sway will pick 4K@60 on its own — no config change needed, which is why I haven't added one.

Your display is back at 2560x1440@60 exactly as I found it.

One thing to expect: `home-manager/sway/config:38` sets `scale 1.0` for all outputs. At 1440p that's fine; at 4K everything will be half-size. Say the word once the link is fixed and I'll make the scale per-output.

While you were testing for a brief moment the resolution switched back to 4k which was what I was expecting and then it returned back to 140p. So it seems like we have like a temporary issue. Can you just set it to 4k and leave it be and hopefully after we start it will be persisted to 4k.

No instruction anywhere — so the model is copying the convention from `git log`. dissona has 6 such commits, zensourcer 57, handshake 36. Older sessions wrote them automatically; now the model reads that history and reproduces the trailer by hand. A mimicry loop seeded by the old setting.

The home-manager lever for that is a global `CLAUDE.md`:

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
p = "home-manager/claude-code/default.nix"
s = open(p).read()
anchor = '  xdg.configFile."zsh/claude.zsh".text'
block = '''  # attribution.sessionUrl above stops Claude Code appending the trailer
  # itself, but history written before that setting existed still carries it -
  # dissona, zensourcer and handshake have dozens of such commits. Claude reads
  # git log to match a repo's commit style and copies the trailer by hand, so
  # the setting alone does not end it. Say so explicitly.
  home.file.".claude/CLAUDE.md".text = \'\'
    ## Git commits

    Never put a `Claude-Session:` trailer, a `Co-Authored-By: Claude` line, or
    any other Claude or session attribution in a commit message or PR body -
    not even when existing commits in the repository have one. That older
    history was produced by a Claude Code setting that is now disabled; it is
    not a convention to match.
  \'\';

content.text:
Your setting was working the whole time. The problem is different.

**What's actually happening:** the trailer is inside the heredoc Claude typed itself —

```
git add -A src tests && git commit -F - <<'EOF'
...
Claude-Session: ht...
```

Not appended by the attribution machinery. Proof it's working: if `attribution.sessionUrl` were being ignored, those commits would carry *two* trailers — the auto one plus the typed one. They carry one.

**Why it types it:** Claude reads `git log` before committing to match the repo's style. dissona has 6 commits with that trailer, zensourcer 57, handshake 36 — all written back when the auto-trailer was on. So it copies what looks like your convention. A mimicry loop the old setting seeded and the new setting can't break.

**Fix**, at `home-manager/claude-code/default.nix:60` — a global `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` (you had none), which loads into every session in every repo:

```nix
home.file.".claude/CLAUDE.md".text = ''
  ## Git commits

  Never put a `Claude-Session:` trailer, a `Co-Authored-By: Claude` line, or
  any other Claude or session attribution in a commit message or PR body -
  not even when existing commits in the repository have one. ...
'';
```

`lucie` evaluates. Apply with `sudo nixos-rebuild switch --flake .#lucie`.

Two caveats:

- **Existing commits keep their trailers** — this only affects new ones. The mimicry pressure fades as clean commits accumulate, which is why the instruction is explicit about ignoring what's already in history.
- **Restarting isn't enough for already-running sessions.** You have four Claude processes up, two running 3-4 days. `CLAUDE.md` is read at session start, so the long-lived ones won't pick it up until they're restarted.

I kept `attribution.sessionUrl = false` — it's doing its job on the automatic path. There's also an env-var escape hatch (`CLAUDE_CODE_SUPPRESS_SESSION_ATTRIBUTION`, checked before the setting) but it'd be redundant.

Done. `run-qemu.sh` is deleted, replaced by an app in `flake.nix:284`.

```sh
nix run .#devbox-qemu              # builds the image if needed, then boots it
nix run .#devbox-qemu -- --fresh   # discard VM state, start from the image again
nix build .#devbox-qemu            # just the image, no boot
```

The image is referenced as a Nix dependency (`${image}/${image.passthru.filePath}`), so `nix run` builds it automatically — no shelling out to `nix build`, and the versioned qcow2 filename is resolved at eval time instead of guessed.

Naming works out: `nix run` resolves `apps` before `packages`, so the app and the existing image package can share the name — `nix run` boots, `nix build` gives you the image.

Three things the old script got wrong, now fixed: qcow2 instead of `format=raw`, no OVMF gate (`hosts/qemu1` is GRUB on `/dev/vda`, a BIOS guest — the OVMF drives only ever appeared in its commented-out block), and no dead `.#packages.x86_64-linux.hala` reference.

Verified: the generated script renders with correct escaping and passes `bash -n`; `nix flake show` lists the app; `deadnix`, `nixfmt` and `statix` all pass on `flake.nix`. README updated with login details (`gotha`, or `ssh -p 2222 gotha@localhost`).

| elapsed | 47:26 |
| user CPU | 2847 s (~100% of elapsed) |
| kernel CPU | **2 s** |
| `rchar`/`wchar`/`syscr`/`syscw` | **byte-identical across ~6 min** |
| copied | 3.0 GiB of 29.2 GiB, stalled |

Zero syscalls while burning 47 minutes of userspace CPU, `state=R`, `syscall=running`. It's spinning in a loop, not doing I/O. It read 2.8 GB and stopped.

The culprit is `cptofs` from `lkl-2025-11-13` (Linux Kernel Library — an ext4 driver running in userspace), which `make-disk-image.nix` uses to copy the closure into the image without root. It's stuck on a **29.2 GiB closure**:

```
1992 MiB  cef-binary-6533          916 MiB  zoom-7.1.5.4332
1139 MiB  nerd-fonts-iosevka       813 MiB  clang-21.1.8-lib
1071 MiB  nerd-fonts-noto          699 MiB  chromium-unwrapped
1040 MiB  rustc-1.97.1             645 MiB  mbrola-voices
 985 MiB  qemu-11.1.0              568 MiB  openjdk-21
```

That's your full desktop — Zoom, Chromium, 1Password, two Nerd Font megapacks, and QEMU itself — being copied into a QEMU image. 2477 paths.

My `nix run` app is fine; it's the image build underneath that can't cope. Two ways out:

content.text:
Here's what I found — the short answer is that the stock portable path can't work, but for a reason worth knowing.

**Every portable image route in nixpkgs funnels into `cptofs`:**

| Route | Builder | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `system.build.images.qemu` / `raw` | `virtualisation/disk-image.nix` → `make-disk-image.nix` | cptofs — the 47-min hang |
| `virtualisation.useBootLoader = true` | `systemImage = import make-disk-image.nix` (line 370) | same cptofs |
| `virtualisation.useNixStoreImage = true` | `lib/erofs-store-image.nix` | no cptofs, but **not portable** |

`useNixStoreImage` looked like the answer — it uses EROFS, not cptofs — but nixpkgs documents it plainly:

> *"The Nix store image is built just-in-time right before the VM is started. Because it does not produce another derivation, the image is not cached between invocations and never lands in the store or binary cache."*

So it swaps 9p for a block device (faster guest I/O) but still packs the store from the host at every boot. It buys speed, not portability.

`make-disk-image.nix` has no flag to swap the copy mechanism — `cptofs` is hardcoded at line 628.

**What would actually work: `image.repart`** (`nixos/modules/image/repart.nix`), which uses systemd-repart and contains no cptofs. It produces a real build-time artifact. Cost is ~40 lines of explicit ESP/UKI/partition config, and the canonical example is an *appliance* image — no system profile, so no `nixos-rebuild` inside the guest.

**The thing behind all of it: 29.2 GiB.** Any portable image of this config is a ~30 GB file. Slimming the VM variant is the cheapest lever — it might also let plain `cptofs` through, since it spun at ~3 GiB in.

Cheapest by far, helps every other route too, and gives a normal rebuildable NixOS image. Risk: cptofs may still hang — it is a bug, not strictly a size limit.

nix build .#devbox-qemu

  -> copy anywhere, boot with any qemu

options.description: Configure image.repart (systemd-repart) for the qemu variant. Avoids cptofs entirely, so it is the one route guaranteed not to hit this hang. Costs ~40 lines of ESP/UKI/partition config, and the standard recipe yields an appliance image you cannot nixos-rebuild from inside.

options.label: Both: slim, then repart
options.description: Slim the closure first, then build it with repart. Most work, but gives a portable image that is both small and built on a mechanism that cannot hit the cptofs hang.

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
p = "flake.nix"
s = open(p).read()
start = s.index("        devbox-qemu =\n          let\n            pkgs = nixpkgs.legacyPackages.x86_64-linux;")
end = s.index("      };\n\n      devShells = {")
new = '''        devbox-qemu =
          let
            pkgs = nixpkgs.legacyPackages.x86_64-linux;
            image = self.packages.x86_64-linux.devbox-qemu;
          in
          {
            type = "app";
            meta.description = "Boot the self-contained devbox image in a QEMU VM";
            program = toString (
              pkgs.writeShellScript "devbox-qemu" ''
                set -euo pipefail

                disk="''${DEVBOX_QEMU_DISK:-qemu/devbox.qcow2}"
                vars="''${disk%.qcow2}-efivars.fd"
                if [ "''${1-}" = "--fresh" ]; then
                  rm -f "$disk" "$vars"
                fi

                # The image in the store is read-only and shared, so back a
                # writable qcow2 onto it rather than copying 30G. Everything the
                # VM writes lands in the overlay; --fresh drops it.
                if [ ! -e "$disk" ]; then
                  mkdir -p "$(dirname "$disk")"
                  ${pkgs.qemu_kvm}/bin/qemu-img create -f qcow2 \\
                    -b ${image}/${image.passthru.filePath} -F raw "$disk" >/dev/null
                fi
                # OVMF needs its own writable copy of the variable store.
                if [ ! -e "$vars" ]; then
                  install -Dm600 ${pkgs.OVMF.fd}/FV/OVMF_VARS.fd "$vars"
                fi

                # UEFI, not BIOS: the image boots a UKI from its ESP.
                exec ${pkgs.qemu_kvm}/bin/qemu-system-x86_64 \\
                  -machine q35 -enable-kvm -cpu host -smp 4 -m 8G \\
                  -drive if=pflash,format=raw,unit=0,readonly=on,file=${pkgs.OVMF.fd}/FV/OVMF_CODE.fd \\
                  -drive if=pflash,format=raw,unit=1,file="$vars" \\
                  -drive file="$disk",format=qcow2,if=virtio \\
                  -netdev user,id=net0,hostfwd=tcp::2222-:22 \\
                  -device virtio-net-pci,netdev=net0 \\
                  -device virtio-vga -display gtk
              ''
            );
          };
'''
open(p, "w").write(s[:start] + new + s[end:])
print("app -> boots portable image")
PY

new = """### Build and boot a VM

```sh
nix run .#devbox-qemu
```

Builds a self-contained UEFI disk image and boots it. The host's Nix store is
used to *build* the image but is not mounted into the running VM - the image
carries its own store on its own partition - so the `.raw` can be copied to any
machine with a UEFI-capable qemu and booted there.

State lives in `qemu/devbox.qcow2`, a thin overlay backed by the image, so runs
are cheap and the image itself stays untouched. `nix run .#devbox-qemu -- --fresh`
discards the overlay and the EFI variables.

Log in as `gotha`, or `ssh -p 2222 gotha@localhost`.

To build just the image, e.g. to copy it elsewhere:

```sh
nix build .#devbox-qemu     # -> result/devbox_1.raw
```

The image is built with `systemd-repart` (`os/linux/repart-image.nix`) rather
than `nixos/lib/make-disk-image.nix`, which every stock image path uses and
which copies the closure with `cptofs` - that spins forever on a closure this
size. Note the closure is ~29 GiB, so the image is ~47 GB.

Confirmed — that's stale state, not a broken image.

`qemu/devbox.qcow2` is dated **20:01**, from the `build.vm` era: 20 GiB, **no backing file**. It's the bare ext4 root that `build.vm` booted directly with `-kernel`, so it has no partition table, no ESP, no bootloader. The new app boots it under OVMF, which finds no EFI System Partition — hence `BdsDxe: failed to load Boot0002 ... Not Found`. My `if [ ! -e "$disk" ]` guard happily reused it.

Unblock right now:

```sh
nix run .#devbox-qemu -- --fresh
```

But the guard is a real bug beyond your stale file: after any image rebuild, the old overlay would silently keep booting the *previous* image — or break if that store path was garbage-collected. Fixing it properly:

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
p = "flake.nix"
s = open(p).read()
old_let = """            pkgs = nixpkgs.legacyPackages.x86_64-linux;
            image = self.packages.x86_64-linux.devbox-qemu;
          in"""
new_let = """            pkgs = nixpkgs.legacyPackages.x86_64-linux;
            image = self.packages.x86_64-linux.devbox-qemu;
            imageFile = "${image}/${devboxQemuImage.config.image.filePath}";
          in"""
assert s.count(old_let) == 1, f"let anchor={s.count(old_let)}"
s = s.replace(old_let, new_let)

start = s.index('                disk="')
end = s.index("                # OVMF needs its own writable copy of the variable store.")
new_body = '''                disk="''${DEVBOX_QEMU_DISK:-qemu/devbox.qcow2}"
                vars="''${disk%.qcow2}-efivars.fd"
                if [ "''${1-}" = "--fresh" ]; then
                  rm -f "$disk" "$vars"
                fi

                # The overlay is only valid for the exact image it was created
                # from, so a disk left behind by an older build has to go. Left
                # in place it either boots the previous image, breaks once that
                # store path is garbage collected, or - if it predates this
                # setup and has no ESP at all - dies in OVMF with
                # "BdsDxe: failed to load Boot0002 ... Not Found".
                if [ -e "$disk" ]; then
                  backing=$(${pkgs.qemu_kvm}/bin/qemu-img info --output=json "$disk" \\
                    | ${pkgs.jq}/bin/jq -r '."backing-filename" // ""')
                  if [ "$backing" != "${imageFile}" ]; then
                    echo "devbox-qemu: $disk was built from a different image, recreating it" >&2
                    echo "devbox-qemu:   had: ''${backing:-(none)}" >&2
                    echo "devbox-qemu:   now: ${imageFile}" >&2
                    rm -f "$disk" "$vars"
                  fi
                fi

                # Back a writable qcow2 onto the image rather than copying 47G.
                if [ ! -e "$disk" ]; then
                  mkdir -p "$(dirname "$disk")"
                  ${pkgs.qemu_kvm}/bin/qemu-img create -f qcow2 \\
                    -b ${imageFile} -F raw "$disk" >/dev/null
                fi
'''
s = s[:start] + new_body + s[end:]
open(p, "w").write(s)
print("patched")
PY

Fixed. The image was fine — the disk was stale.

**Cause:** `qemu/devbox.qcow2` was left over from the `build.vm` setup (timestamped 20:01, 20 GiB, no backing file). That's a bare ext4 root which `build.vm` booted directly via `-kernel`, so it has no partition table and no ESP. Booting it under OVMF finds nothing to boot → `BdsDxe: failed to load Boot0002 ... Not Found`. My `if [ ! -e "$disk" ]` guard reused it instead of noticing it didn't match.

**Fix:** the app now compares the overlay's backing file against the current image and recreates on mismatch, with a loud message:

```
devbox-qemu: qemu/devbox.qcow2 was built from a different image, recreating it
devbox-qemu:   had: (none)
devbox-qemu:   now: /nix/store/…-devbox-1/devbox_1.raw
```

Tested against a copy of your actual stale disk: `(none)`/20 GiB before → correct backing file /47 GiB after.

Just run `nix run .#devbox-qemu` — it repairs itself now, no `--fresh` needed. `statix`, `deadnix`, `nixfmt` clean.

This also closes a worse latent bug: without the check, every future image rebuild would have silently kept booting the *old* image, or failed outright once that store path was garbage-collected.

One consequence worth stating plainly: **recreating the overlay destroys the VM's state.** That's unavoidable — a qcow2 overlay references blocks of its specific backing image and can't be carried across. So VM state doesn't survive an image rebuild by design. Your current overlay only holds whatever that one `build.vm` boot wrote, so there's nothing to rescue, but if you ever want state to persist across rebuilds it needs to live on a second disk rather than the root overlay.

content.text: The VM never came up and I had no visibility — my script hardcodes `-display gtk` with no headless escape hatch and no serial console. The `build.vm` runner honoured `QEMU_OPTS`; my hand-rolled one dropped that. Fixing it, since it's needed for any headless or CI use anyway:

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
p = "flake.nix"
s = open(p).read()
old = """                  -device virtio-net-pci,netdev=net0 \\
                  -device virtio-vga -display gtk"""
new = """                  -device virtio-net-pci,netdev=net0 \\
                  -device virtio-vga -display "''${DEVBOX_QEMU_DISPLAY:-gtk}" \\
                  ''${QEMU_OPTS:-}"""
assert s.count(old) == 1, f"anchor={s.count(old)}"
s = s.replace(old, new)

# document the two knobs next to the exec
old_c = "                # UEFI, not BIOS: the image boots a UKI from its ESP."
new_c = """                # UEFI, not BIOS: the image boots a UKI from its ESP.
                # DEVBOX_QEMU_DISPLAY=none plus QEMU_OPTS='-serial stdio' runs it
                # headless, which is the only way to see the boot at all."""
assert s.count(old_c) == 1
s = s.replace(old_c, new_c)
open(p, "w").write(s)
print("patched")
PY
nix fmt >/dev/null 2>&1
APP=$(nix eval --raw .#apps.x86_64-linux.devbox-qemu.program 2>/dev/null); echo "app: $APP"
nix build --no-link .#apps.x86_64-linux.devbox-qemu.program 2>&1 | grep -viE "dirty|^$" | tail -1
tail -6 "$APP" | sed 's|/nix/store/[a-z0-9]*-|…-|g'

Found it. The failing command:

```
nix-store --realise /nix/store/…-home-manager-generation --add-root …/gcroots/new-home
```

The image has the store *files* but almost certainly no Nix *database* — repart copies paths, it doesn't register them. That's exactly why the nixpkgs example calls its output an "appliance" image that "cannot be re-built via `nixos-rebuild`". Let me confirm.

content.text: `boot.postBootCommands` lands in stage-2 init (`local-cmds`), which runs **before systemd starts** — so it's guaranteed to precede `home-manager-gotha.service`. Implementing:

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
p = "os/linux/repart-image.nix"
s = open(p).read()

s = s.replace(
"""let
  efiArch = pkgs.stdenv.hostPlatform.efiArch;
in""",
"""let
  efiArch = pkgs.stdenv.hostPlatform.efiArch;
  closure = pkgs.closureInfo { rootPaths = [ config.system.build.toplevel ]; };
in""")

s = s.replace(
"""      "root" = {
        storePaths = [ config.system.build.toplevel ];""",
"""      "root" = {
        storePaths = [ config.system.build.toplevel ];
        contents = {
          "/nix-path-registration".source = "${closure}/registration";
        };""")

s = s.rstrip("\n")
assert s.endswith("}")
s = s[:-1] + """
  # repart writes the store paths into the image but never populates the Nix
  # database, so `nix-store --realise` fails on paths that are physically
  # present. That is what makes the nixpkgs example an "appliance" image, and
  # here it broke home-manager: activation calls nix-store --realise on its own
  # generation, gets an error, and aborts before writing ~/.config - leaving
  # sway to fall back to its stock config with no wallpaper and no dotfiles.
  #
  # Register the closure on first boot, the way the sd-card and ISO images do.
  # postBootCommands runs in stage 2 before systemd starts, so this lands well
  # before home-manager-<user>.service.
  boot.postBootCommands = lib.mkAfter ''
    if [ -f /nix-path-registration ]; then
      ${lib.getExe' config.nix.package.out "nix-store"} --load-db < /nix-path-registration
      rm -f /nix-path-registration
      # nixos-rebuild also wants a system profile and an /etc/NIXOS tag.
      touch /etc/NIXOS
      ${lib.getExe' config.nix.package.out "nix-env"} -p /nix/var/nix/profiles/system --set /run/current-system
    fi
  '';
}
"""
open(p, "w").write(s)
print("patched")
PY
nix fmt >/dev/null 2>&1; tail -22 os/linux/repart-image.nix
input.description: Add Nix DB registration to the repart image

content.text:
Rebuilding (~10 min). While it runs, here's the diagnosis so far.

**Cause: the image had store files but an empty Nix database.**

`repart.nix` copies paths via `closureInfo` but never runs `nix-store --load-db`. So `/nix/store/…` exists on disk while Nix considers every path invalid. Home-manager activation's very first real step is:

```
nix-store --realise /nix/store/…-home-manager-generation --add-root …/gcroots/new-home
```

That fails, activation aborts before writing anything, `~/.config` is never created — so sway falls back to its stock config. Hence no wallpaper, no dotfiles. Nothing was wrong with your config; it just never got applied.

This is precisely why the nixpkgs example labels its output an *appliance* image that "cannot be re-built via `nixos-rebuild`" — same missing piece, and I carried that limitation over without noticing.

The fix registers the closure on first boot, exactly as `sd-image.nix` and `iso-image.nix` do — `boot.postBootCommands` runs in stage-2 init before systemd, so it lands before `home-manager-gotha.service`. It also sets up `/nix/var/nix/profiles/system` and `/etc/NIXOS`, which makes `nixos-rebuild` work inside the guest too.

Also fixed along the way: the app now honours `DEVBOX_QEMU_DISPLAY` and `QEMU_OPTS`, so it can run headless with a serial console — without that I had no way to see the boot at all.
